Fifth Commandment
FIFTH ko-MAND-ment
noun (moral law)
English “commandment” for the Hebrew mitsvah, a precept or charge; the fifth word of the Decalogue, “Honour thy father and thy mother.”

Biblical Definition

The fifth commandment is the first word of the second table of the law: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Exo 20:12). Standing at the head of our duties to men, it is the root of all lawful authority and obedience. The honour owed to father and mother is, in the Reformed reading of the law, the pattern and fountain of every relation of superior and inferior—in the family, the church, the commonwealth, and the workplace—so that this one precept teaches reverence, submission, and dutiful love wherever God has set authority over us. The apostle calls it “the first commandment with promise” (Eph 6:1-3), for to its keeping is annexed the pledge of length of days and well-being, a promise the New Testament applies to the children of the church. This complementarian order is not an arrangement of human convenience but a created and commanded structure: God ordains fathers and mothers, magistrates and pastors, masters and elders, and binds the conscience to honour them in the Lord. The commandment is fulfilled and adorned in Christ, the perfect Son, who was subject to His earthly parents, obedient to His heavenly Father unto death, and now reigns as the Head over all. He keeps the law His people break and supplies in His obedience the honour we have withheld. Thus the fifth commandment both governs the home and points to the gospel, where the obedient Son secures the inheritance for adopted children.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Decalogue's charge to honour father and mother, the first commandment with promise and the root of lawful authority.

FIFTH COMMANDMENT, noun (moral law). From the Hebrew mitsvah, a precept; the fifth word of the Decalogue.

The precept requiring honour and obedience to father and mother.

The head of the second table, governing all relations of authority and submission.

The first commandment with promise: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.” (Exo 20:12)

Figuratively, the foundation of order in family, church, and commonwealth.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:12 — "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee."

Eph 6:2 — "Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;)"

Eph 6:1 — "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right."

Col 3:20 — "Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord."

Modern Corruption

The commandment is pressed hard by an age that resents all settled authority and the ordered structure of the family.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the spirit of the age corrodes it by exalting personal autonomy above every duty owed to parents and lawful superiors, treating honour as optional and authority as suspect. The principle to recover is that God Himself ordains the offices of father and mother, and that to honour them in the Lord is the root of all rightful order in family, church, and state.

The recovery is glad submission within God's created structure. The commandment carries a promise, binding obedience to blessing, and it is no burden but a fountain of well-being. It is fulfilled in Christ the perfect Son, obedient to His parents and to His Father unto death, whose righteousness covers the dishonour His people have shown and secures the inheritance for the adopted children of God.

Hebrew Roots

The commandment rests on the Hebrew words for honour and for father and mother within the Decalogue.

expand to see more

kabed — to honour; literally to count weighty, to give due reverence.

'ab — father; head of the household and of authority.

'em — mother; honoured equally with the father in the precept.

mitsvah — commandment, precept, charge from God.

Greek timaō — to honour, the verb Paul uses in citing the commandment.

Usage

"Of the literal charge to honour one's father and mother."

"Of the broader duty of reverence to all lawful authority God has set over us."

"Of the commandment's promise of length of days and well-being to the obedient."
